content: When a mother smiles and responds to her child’s smiles, the child begins to learn how to communicate. The mother, in turn, observes her child responding to her actions. Fathers should also be encouraged to engage in communication with their newborns. Infants communicate their needs through movements, sounds, and cries, and they develop trust when caregivers respond to these signals. Breastfeeding on demand strengthens this interaction and builds trust. Babies show signs of hunger by becoming fussy, sucking on their hands, or turning their heads toward the breast. Recognizing these cues allows mothers to identify hunger before the baby starts crying. From birth, babies learn through play. Providing opportunities for them to see, hear, move their arms and legs freely, and touch their caregivers is essential. Gentle soothing, stroking, and holding the baby, especially through skin-to-skin contact, fosters a sense of security. Looking into the baby’s eyes and talking to them, particularly during breastfeeding, is an excellent way to communicate. For infants aged 1 week to 6 months, play involves reaching for and grasping objects, looking at their hands and feet as if discovering them, and exploring objects with their mouths. The mouth is a sensitive tool for learning about textures and temperatures. Caregivers should ensure that objects are clean and large enough to prevent choking. Encouraging the child to follow a colorful object with their eyes and reach for it helps develop coordination. Simple household items like wooden spoons or plastic bowls, as well as homemade toys like shaker rattles, can stimulate interest. Infants also enjoy seeing faces and interacting with family members who hold and carry them. Communication at this stage involves responding to the baby’s sounds, such as squeals and laughs, and copying these sounds to encourage interaction. This helps caregivers pay close attention to the baby’s needs and interests, fostering a deeper understanding of the child’s communication. Smiling, laughing, and talking to the baby, as well as imitating their sounds and movements, create a foundation for future conversations. For infants aged 6 to 9 months, play becomes more exploratory. Babies enjoy making noises by banging objects, passing items between their hands, and dropping them to observe the results. While this behavior may frustrate busy caregivers, it is important to understand that the child is learning through experimentation. Caregivers can support this by providing safe household items for the child to handle, such as containers with lids or metal pots and spoons. Communication at this stage involves responding to the baby’s sounds and showing interest in their discoveries. Babies begin to recognize their names and respond to them, which reinforces their sense of identity within the family. For infants aged 9 to 12 months, play continues to be a time of exploration and learning. Babies enjoy games like peek-a-boo and discovering hidden objects. They also begin to understand the names of objects and connect words to their meanings, such as associating the word “bird” with a bird in a tree. Caregivers can encourage this by naming objects and people, and by teaching simple gestures like waving “bye-bye.” For children aged 12 months to 2 years, play becomes more active as they explore their environment. They enjoy simple household or natural items, such as stacking objects or placing items into containers and taking them out. Encouragement and assistance from caregivers help children develop new skills and build confidence. Repetition of new games or skills brings joy and reinforces learning. Communication at this stage involves asking simple questions, responding to the child’s attempts to talk, and engaging in conversations during daily activities like feeding and bathing. Children begin to understand and follow simple directions, and they may say a few words like “water” or “ball.” Looking at pictures and talking about them helps prepare children for reading and improves their language skills. For children aged 2 years and older, play involves naming objects, counting, and sorting items by color, shape, or size. Caregivers can encourage learning by asking questions like “How many?” and by playing games that involve counting. Children enjoy drawing with chalk or sticks and solving simple puzzles made from household items. Communication at this stage includes encouraging the child to talk, answering their questions, and teaching them stories, songs, and games. Listening to and understanding stories helps children learn about right and wrong, and they often imitate the behavior of older siblings and family members. Gentle correction and positive reinforcement are more effective than scolding, as they help children learn without feeling ashamed. Throughout all stages, caregivers should show affection, respond to the child’s interests, and praise their efforts to learn new skills. Engaging in play and communication activities strengthens the bond between caregivers and children, fostering emotional, social, and intellectual development.
